title: Storm Lala: Hawaii braces for potential first direct hit by a hurricane in 34 years
description: Hawaii is bracing for what could be its first direct hit from a hurricane since 1992, as category one storm Lala churns off its coast.Packing 75mph (1
body: Hawaii is bracing for what could be its first direct hit from a hurricane since 1992, as category one storm Lala churns off its coast.Packing 75mph (120km/h) winds, Lala gained hurricane strength on Saturday. In a worst-case scenario, it could dump up to 25in (63cm) of rain on Big Island and produce a 3ft storm surge. A hurricane warning is in effect for Big Island, while Maui County, Oahu, Kauai and Niihau are under tropical storm warnings. Officials have told residents to prepare for "life-threatening" conditions, including floods and mudslides. The storm is expected to either make landfall or pass close to the southern tip of Big Island on Saturday, before continuing west.The last time a hurricane made landfall on Hawaii's Big Island was 155 years ago, according to the Associated Press news agency.Over the weekend, Lala will continue moving westwards, and may weaken into a tropical storm, with the centre passing just below Hawaii's other islands.Hawaii Governor Josh Green warned residents to brace for "an incredible amount of water"."Damaging winds, heavy rain, flash flooding and dangerous surf are possible across the state through the weekend," he posted on X.Dozens of flights have been cancelled.At Ellison Onizuka Kona International - Big Island's largest airport - 40% of flights were grounded, according to flightaware.com. Some 80% of flights were called off at its other main airport, Hilo International.The more dire forecasts from the National Weather Service (NWS) have been issued for areas within Big Island's south-east. "Major rainfall flooding may prompt many evacuations and rescues," the NWS said, adding that rivers and tributaries "may rapidly overflow their banks in multiple places".Nearly 37,000 customers had lost electricity on Hawaii as of Saturday afternoon, according to the website poweroutage.us.Meteorologist Jennifer Myers, who lives in Hilo, eastern Big Island, said landslides had already cut off some roads, while power lines had been ripped down by falling trees."I'm looking at the river right now, and it's really, really high," she told the BBC about the view from her apartment of the Wailuku River as it meets Hilo Bay. "The bay that's usually blue is like blood red right now because of all the sediment and river water in it."

schema.headline: Storm Lala: Hawaii braces for potential first direct hit by a hurricane in 34 years

title: Met Police apologises for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims
description: The Metropolitan Police has apologised after it inadvertently disclosed email addresses of around 140 people who say they were sexually abused by the
body: The Metropolitan Police has apologised after it inadvertently disclosed email addresses of around 140 people who say they were sexually abused by the late Harrods owner Mohamed Al Fayed.Scotland Yard confirmed to the BBC it copied in all those who had signed up to receive a monthly email update for victims instead of blind copying them.The update revealed a further three suspects in their 70s and 80s had been interviewed under caution, bringing the total number interviewed to seven.The force said it had referred itself to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO). It is considering providing further support to the victims along with additional safeguards.A Met Police spokesperson told the BBC a monthly update sent to victims on 11 August regarding Operation Cornpoppy had contained details of progress in the investigation.Operation Cornpoppy is the Metropolitan Police investigation into people who may have facilitated or enabled sexual offending by Al Fayed.The spokesperson said: "Due to human error, recipients' email addresses were visible to others on the distribution list. The issue was identified quickly and immediate action was taken."We understand the impact this may have on victims and sincerely apologise. Everyone affected was contacted directly on the day of the incident."The incident is being investigated as a matter of priority, and we are reviewing our processes to help prevent a similar breach from happening again."The force said the breach affected victims who had opted in to receive updates from the investigation team, but recipients had been split into smaller groups, meaning email addresses were only visible within those groups rather than across the entire cohort.The BBC understands around 140 people have signed up to the updates. The force has previously said 154 victims have reported allegations connected to Al Fayed and that supporting survivors remains at the heart of the investigation.It said the incident had been formally recorded within the investigation records and they would continue to monitor the circumstances and impact of the breach, including reviewing alternative methods of updating victims that would reduce the risk of human error.The force added that victim-survivors remained its priority and said it was committed to providing updates to those involved in the investigation.The latest disclosure is likely to raise fresh questions about the Metropolitan Police's handling of sensitive survivor information.Campaigners have repeatedly stressed the importance of protecting the identities of people involved in investigations into sexual abuse and trafficking because of the potential impact on victims' wellbeing and privacy.Joanna Brittan, from Devon, who spoke to the BBC after waiving her automatic lifelong right to anonymity, discovered her email address had been disclosed to dozens of other survivors after an update about Operation Cornpoppy was sent to multiple recipients with their email addresses visible.In an email seen by the BBC, Brittan wrote to senior officers saying her email address had "been disclosed to 42 other survivors, and I have likewise been given access to their email addresses".She described the incident as particularly serious because recipients were identifiable as people connected to a highly sensitive criminal investigation."I consider this to be a further personal data breach by the Metropolitan Police Service," she wrote.Brittan said she had previously been offered compensation for another data breach by the Met, after they disclosed sensitive information about her first police interview by mistake to two people in Australia.Speaking about the latest breach, the 61-year-old told the BBC: "It's very shocking because they were meant to have learned all lessons and it would never happen again. "And although the first one was far more egregious because it was very sensitive data that was sent to Australia, I was promised that they had learned and the same thing couldn't happen again.She added that many of Al Fayed's alleged victims would be distressed by the breach, saying: "For me, it's more of the same, really, and deeply re abusive, to be honest. It's unbelievable."Dame Jasvinder Sanghera, the advocate for survivors of alleged abuse by Al Fayed, told the BBC: "I have had so many contacts today from survivors who have told me that they feel violated by the police in a space where there is already a lack of confidence in the police investigation."They said they received an insipid apology five hours later and, I am sorry, it is just not good enough."Brittan first reported allegations to police in 2017.According to correspondence previously supplied to the BBC, she alleged she was sexually abused by Ahmed Obaidly, a former United Arab Emirates diplomat and associate of Al Fayed, after working for a company linked to the UAE royal family in the early 1990s.The Met has said the original report, made to Devon and Cornwall Police in 2017, was transferred to London because the alleged offending took place within its jurisdiction. It said the case was initially investigated as a rape allegation against Obaidly, who died in 2015.The force has also said criminal allegations concerning Mohamed Al Fayed were made in 2024 and now form part of Operation Cornpoppy, which remains ongoing.In correspondence previously provided to the BBC, the Met said: "The live investigation into those who could have facilitated or enabled Mohamed Al Fayed's offending continues."The force added that victim-survivors remained its priority and said it was committed to providing updates to those involved in the investigation.The latest incident comes shortly after the ICO took enforcement action against the Metropolitan Police over two unrelated data breaches.In a decision published on 5 August, the watchdog issued the force with a reprimand and enforcement notice after concluding it had failed to put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal information.The ICO said its investigation had uncovered "serious and ongoing shortcomings" in data protection training.It also found wider weaknesses in policies, procedures and assurance arrangements for handling sensitive personal data.One breach involved an officer disclosing a stalking victim's new address and telephone number to her alleged stalker.As part of its enforcement notice, the ICO ordered the Metropolitan Police to improve its data protection training compliance, monitoring and governance arrangements.

schema.headline: Met Police apologises for data breach involving alleged Al Fayed victims

title: Finlay Tarling: Cycling union CPA calls for better helmets for racers
description: The cyclists' union has expressed "fury" over the death of British rider Fin Tarling    during Friday's stage of the Volta a Portugal.The 19-year-old
body: The cyclists' union has expressed "fury" over the death of British rider Fin Tarling    during Friday's stage of the Volta a Portugal.The 19-year-old NSN Cycling rider reportedly collided with a vehicle not involved in the race.And the union's president Adam Hansen told BBC Sport there needs to be better helmet safety as cyclists hit record-breaking speeds during races."We are speechless and filled with anger," said the Cyclistes Professionnels Associes (CPA) on social media."It is not right that a young athlete's life should end this way, and we are furious that even today it is still not possible to prevent such serious accidents."We share in the grief of his family, friends, team, and everyone who knew Finlay. Rest in peace, young rider; we pray for you, and we will carry you in our hearts."Tarling was the younger brother of Josh, a time trial specialist for British super team Netcompany Ineos, who has won a stage of the Giro d'Italia and a European Time Trial title.Fin Tarling himself had finished strongly in the time trial a few days earlier in the race he would never finish.He was part of a new generation of male and female British riders on the World Tour who grew up on the success of highly decorated road cyclists, such as Mark Cavendish, Chris Froome and Lizzie Deignan, during a golden decade for British participation in the sport from 2012.Just like all young professionals, Fin spent hours every day trying to extract as much performance as possible. But he was known to love every element of cycling and was always in the saddle.His parents, Michael and Dawn, frequently attended races and even set up their own team in their home in Ceredigion, west Wales.BBC Sport understands organisers are considering a tribute to Tarling at the men's Tour of Britain, which starts on 2 September.As tributes to Tarling flowed in on Saturday the investigation into a "collision between the cyclist and a light goods vehicle" had begun, according to the National Republican Guard in Portugal.Portuguese media are reporting the driver is unlikely to face charges., externalCycling might not seem as dangerous as motorsport or boxing, but on descents out on public roads lycra-clad competitors can reach up to 60mph protected by nothing other than a helmet.Although reporting on incidents has grown, the feeling in the sport is that there are more fatalities now as speeds increase.In a sport where the peloton used to pick its moments to exert energy, today's racing is "full gas from the word go" as riders try to find pace advantages in all areas of stages.At the Tour de France last month the record average speed was broken on stage 11 as riders reached 50.91km/h (31.6mph)., externalSix riders have died during road races in the past three years.These include high-profile fatalities such as Switzerland's Muriel Furrer, who was not spotted leaving the road during the 2024 Road World Championships' junior road race, leaving a head injury untreated for more than an hour.Furrer's compatriot Gino Mader was killed a year earlier during the Tour de Suisse following a high-speed crash on a descent.Tarling's death is the first in a road race in 2026 and the full circumstances are yet to be disclosed."One thing we have to look at is helmets," Hansen told BBC Sport."They need a major upgrade. Bike helmets only need to meet standard testing like all helmets, EU standard CE EN 1078 is only rated for 19.5km/h and I do not believe this is enough for road racing."BBC Sport has contacted the sport's world governing body the UCI for comment on helmet standards.There are hazards everywhere along a road course in cycling and it is impossible to control exactly what lies around any corner across a stage which could be in excess of 100 miles.In the biggest races in the sport, such as three-week Grand Tour the Tour de France, some stages take place on fully closed roads, but many World Tour events use a 'rolling roadblock'.This is where police and organisers use motorbikes and cars to ensure the road is clear at certain junctions and temporarily enforce a closure in theory until all competitors have passed through.It is a costly procedure which often involves more than 30 vehicles.It is understood Friday's stage was using a rolling roadblock and that Tarling was adrift of the peloton, which is common for a rider who does not need to keep pace with the main bunch after a certain distance, or who may need to fall back for a team service car."The organisation is [generally] very good, but what happened [on Friday] is a bit of a hole in the system," added Hansen."When the breakaway or the main group goes past, sometimes the drivers [from the general public] think that's the whole race. But in fact there are riders behind and on some mountain stages the difference can be 45 minutes."If people do not know racing, then they just naturally think the race has passed and go on to the course, where in fact there can be many groups."There have been many examples where riders have had collisions or close calls with cars entering a live stage route regardless of the type of closure.German Max Schachmann was hit by a car during Il Lombardia in 2020, and the 2023 Tour Feminin des Pyrenees was cancelled before the final stage after riders refused to compete following several close calls with vehicles on the route., externalHansen added: "To close every single road and driveway is difficult and it gets to the point how little risk the organisers want to take and if it's even possible for them to have people at all those points."

schema.headline: Finlay Tarling: Cycling union CPA calls for better helmets for racers

title: Fire services 'under pressure' as evacuated residents still not home
description: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, A total of 38 homes have been destroyed or damaged in StourbridgeBySusie RackWest MidlandsJoan CumminsRep
body: Image source, EPA/ShutterstockImage caption, A total of 38 homes have been destroyed or damaged in StourbridgeBySusie RackWest MidlandsJoan CumminsReporting fromin Stourbridge and Christopher SteersReporting fromin Stoke-on-TrentEleven major fires in the past 48 hours and 43 new wildfires since Friday have left services under "incredible pressure", a fire boss has said.Phil Garrigan from the National Fire Chief's Council (NFCC) said major incidents had been declared across the UK, including in Stourbridge, Sandwell, Pershore and Stoke-on-Trent in the West Midlands, as well as in Hampshire and South Wales.In Stourbridge, 38 houses have been destroyed or damaged by the fires, with some residents left unable to return home.West Midlands Fire Service set up a meeting point on Saturday where residents would be told if their house had been damaged or totally destroyed in the blaze and if it was safe to go back.West Midlands Assistant Chief Fire Officer Simon Barry told residents the fire there was under control and they were just dampening down hot spots. He said as far as the service was concerned, homes were no longer at risk and he hoped some residents whose homes had been unaffected would be able to move back on Saturday evening.In a recorded online briefing, Dudley Council chief executive Balvinder Hera stressed residents should not return home until explicitly told they could do so.She said decisions to reopen roads were being taken on a street-by-street basis, with the council working closely with emergency services.Police were keen to hear from people with information or video footage that could assist inquiries and had asked the public not to speculate on the fire's cause, she said.An online fund, external has been set up by the council to allow people to donate to those affected.Image source, EPAImage caption, Three hundred residents were evacuated in Stourbridge, with many still not homeWest Midlands Fire and Rescue Service was alerted to the large grass fire near Stourbridge Golf Club in the Racecourse Lane area just before 13:30 BST on Thursday.More than 100 firefighters fought the flames across an area of 500 acres, with hotspots remaining on Saturday.John Moore was asked to leave his home on Osmaston Road as fire spread through grass and woodland about half a mile away.He said he was now visiting the cordon four times a day to seek information."It's absolutely shocking. We can get no answers about when we can go back," he said.The house he shares with his 86-year-old wife, who is partially bedridden, was not damaged, but he has only been permitted to visit it to pick up medication.Moore said: "There's probably about 60 other people who are normally here by the side of me every day asking, 'can we go?'."Image caption, John Moore has visited the cordon multiple times each day to seek answersSimon Tuhill from West Midlands Fire Service said 19 properties had been "completely destroyed", with a further 19 damaged.He said specialist investigators were on the scene and working with police to try to "triangulate down where the fire started".Other residents who have lost everything gathered at a cordon at the corner of Worcester Road and Racecourse Lane, frustrated by the lack of information and not being allowed to see what had become of their homes.One man told the BBC he had met Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Friday when he visited the region, saying Burnham had promised to personally intervene to help his family get their passports.A woman described suffering horrific flashbacks and claimed it had taken 40 minutes for a fire engine to respond to her emergency call.Meanwhile, A-level student Dominic Abdullah was forced to flee shortly after he had got his results on Thursday."I thought the day couldn't get any more big, any more significant," he said.Figure caption, Student evacuates home after receiving A-level resultsA national government alert sent out by the government on Friday warned people not to light anything that might spark a fire.Garrigan said the NFCC had asked politicians to highlight the risks fire services were  facing, with control room operators dealing with "thousands and thousands of calls".He said services had been unable to immediately meet demand at points during the busiest 24-hour period from Thursday afternoon."They'd asked for maybe 10 additional appliances to come in nationally, and we weren't able to provide them with the full 10 in the first instance," he said.He added firefighters were "still seeing fires occur through maybe carelessness or deliberate action".Image caption, Marie Leese's treasured garden was destroyed by flamesElsewhere in the West Midlands, in Goldenhill, Stoke-on-Trent, four homes in Sandyford were destroyed on Thursday, with other nearby properties damaged.Marie Leese escaped the fire with just her dog and her phone, but her beloved garden on Maureen Avenue was destroyed, including a summer house built by her husband before he died."It was like the scenes of the Blitz, just a blazing inferno, the flames were moving so quickly," she said."I feel fortunate that I've been allowed back, but the house across the road still has hotspots and is destroyed."She said she was too terrified to sleep, because the neighbouring house "keeps reigniting".Two people have been arrested by Staffordshire Police on suspicion of arson in connection with the incident. In Clun, Shropshire, firefighters spent the night tackling a fire on Black Hill.An emergency presence was expected in the area for some time as hot spots were put out. "As you can imagine, the thick forestry makes this type of fire incredibly challenging to tackle," said Clun Fire Station on social media. And in the Peak District a fire in Totley Rail Tunnel between Totley, Sheffield, and Grindleford, has led to all lines being closed.Get in touchTell us which stories we should cover in Birmingham and the Black Country

title: Leavitt and Ocasio-Cortez spark conversation on challenges of family and career
description: US women in politics spark conversation about balancing family and careerImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, White House Press Secretary Karoline
body: US women in politics spark conversation about balancing family and careerImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt and Congresswoman Alexandra Ocasio-Cortez have both spoken in recent days about balancing their careers with motherhoodByMadeline HalpertLast summer, Representative Sara Jacobs would run up to her office to give herself injections of hormones before rushing back to Congress for a session with her fellow lawmakers.The shots were for the second round of freezing her eggs, a medical procedure that can give women more time to have children."It was an empowering decision that gave me more agency," the 37-year-old said, adding that the process was challenging."Your body hurts. Your hormones are crazy. It's kind of like puberty and menopause at the same time," she said.Jacobs announced she was beginning the egg freezing process in 2021, at a time where she said few lawmakers were discussing the topic in the halls of Congress. The process - which can cost more than $10,000 and is rarely covered by insurance - involves doctors harvesting eggs from the ovaries and freezing them for a future pregnancy.This week, Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez announced she too was beginning the process of freezing her eggs, documenting the daily mechanics of giving herself hormone shots on social media.Figure caption, Watch: Key moments from Karoline Leavitt's White House tenureThe left-wing Democrat's announcement sparked a conversation about the challenges of balancing motherhood and a demanding career, the same week that White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt announced she would be leaving the Trump administration to spend more time with her family, including her infant."The truth is since returning to the White House after the birth of my daughter, I have felt in my heart that I cannot be the best mum my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy, and attention required of the White House Press Secretary," Leavitt said.Several women with busy careers spoke to the BBC about the challenges of juggling their work with motherhood in the only industrialised nation that does not mandate paid parental leave.Less than a quarter of workers in the US have access to paid family leave through their employer, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Over 120 nations around the world - including all European countries - provide paid maternity leave.In the US, women are increasingly having children at older ages, while more are choosing not to have children at all. From 2016 to 2023, the average age of all mothers giving birth in the US rose from 28.7 to 29.6, according to a 2025 report from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.Image source, Jennifer Morris photographyImage caption, Michele Heisler (left) says raising her children while working as a professor of medicine meant long nights, and lots of helpMichele Heisler, a professor of internal medicine at the University of Michigan, gave birth to her first child after going back to medical school at the age of 30. She was pregnant with her son during her third year of medical school.Heisler, who serves as medical director for nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights, said she has only been able to dedicate enough time to her career because of access to resources - including nannies - and a husband who is an equal partner in parenting."Unless it's clear that both are equal parents, [child rearing] is always going to fall on the woman, and then you're going to have to take a step back in some way," Heisler said.Heisler said a flexible schedule is what allowed her to pursue her career to the fullest - staying up late at night to work and waking up sometimes at 05:00 to get her research done - so she could spend time with her children.Image source, Supplied by Seema PatelImage caption, Legal scholar Seema Patel says she stays up late to finish work after her children are in bedSeema Patel, an associate professor of law at UC Law San Francisco, also stays up late at night to try to finish her work so she doesn't have to miss moments with her children."The reality is that these years in your kids' lives are so fleeting, and I'm super aware of the time," she said.Patel worked for San Francisco's Office of Labor Standards Enforcement, which became the first local government in the US to pass a law requiring employers to provide paid parental leave.But through her career as a workers' rights lawyer, she has seen many lower-wage workers and parents who are not lucky enough to have access to paid time off.When Patel began working as a federal attorney, her boss advised her to save up her vacation days in case she eventually wanted to have children and needed to take leave. She ended up taking the advice."I was a brand new, young attorney who had not even contemplated that stage of my life, but I had to in that moment, face that question of - I better be saving my vacation days," she said.But even with some maternity leave and a dedicated partner, as her children - now ages 13, 11 and 7 - have grown older, the work-life juggling act remains a challenge."I have a high producing job," she said. "How can I do that while also being there for my kids and attentive to them? I don't have an answer."Image source, Supplied by Sara JacobsImage caption, Congresswoman Sara Jacobs documented her journey freezing her eggs on social mediaFor now, Jacobs, who has completed two rounds of egg freezing, plans to hold off on having children while her job requires her to fly across the country from California to Washington."Figuring out how to be a mom when I'm gone half the time across the country, it's logistically complicated," she said.Jacobs said she was impressed by her fellow lawmakers who have managed to make it work. Only a handful of women have given birth while in Congress, while a few dozen lawmakers are mothers to children under the age of 18.The federal government, like many US employers, does not offer paid parental leave, Jacobs noted."Both Congress and the general American workplace were designed by and for men who had often stay-at-home spouses who handled all of the domestic work," she said. "It's going to take a lot of work for us to create a society where the domestic work is really shared equally between women and men."In the meanwhile, Jacobs feels reassured to have a back-up plan for whenever she does feel she can fit children into her busy career."I hope to be able to do that one day, but I just haven't figured the time is right just yet," she said.

schema.headline: Leavitt and Ocasio-Cortez spark conversation on challenges of family and career

title: 'I started in my 20s and made £8,000': Why women are often better investors than men
description: Image source, Teleri EvansImage caption, Teleri Evans used her investments to put a deposit down on her first homeByWill SmalePhil Leake and Jess Carr
body: Image source, Teleri EvansImage caption, Teleri Evans used her investments to put a deposit down on her first homeByWill SmalePhil Leake and Jess CarrBBC NewsWomen who invest their money get slightly higher long-term returns than men, new analysis suggests.But only about a quarter of UK women have investments, compared with about 40% of men, a separate report shows.We've looked at the data behind these trends, which reveal some surprising differences in how men and women approach investing.Teleri Evans was 25 when she began saving into a Help To Buy ISA then a couple of years later she took out a stocks and shares Lifetime ISA. By 33, she had £40,000 saved - with £8,000 of it returns on her investments."I saved aggressively, and lived at my mum's for half of that time, so I could save as close as possible to the maximum £4,000 per year into Lifetime ISA," she says.The civil servant from Cardiff used the money towards a house deposit earlier this year with her partner.Only 26% of UK women invest, but that this falls to 23% for those under 45, according to a study by consumer finance website Boring Money. In contrast, 41% of all men invest, which holds steady at 40% of those under 45.So why are fewer women investing than men?It can be "largely attributed to culture", according to Gillian Fleming, co-founder and managing director of UK-based Mint Ventures, a women-led angel investment firm."Men historically have been more likely to make family investment decisions, and women have also historically not owned the balance of wealth, but that is changing now," she says."Also, money and wealth creation is not a topic that women often discuss, and we would like to change that."Women who investTeleri says she has noticed a shift of late. "Investing is definitely something that women are talking about more, which is always a good thing," she says. "That's the case with my friendship group."When women do invest in stocks and shares, analysis by Fidelity International found that over three years its female personal investing customers recorded cumulative returns of 50%, compared with 47% for men. The analysis does not identify the reason for the difference, but why may it be the case?One possible clue to women's slightly higher long-term returns lies in how often they buy and sell their investments, with Barclays data showing that women trade around half as frequently as men.This could be because women are more patient and risk averse, says Joanna Floyd, business psychologist at London-based The Work Psychologists. "Studies show that male investors trade more than women, chasing higher returns, but women actually get higher returns," she says."The restraint that keeps women out of the market in the first place is the very same thing that rewards them once they are in it."That more cautious approach to risk can be seen beyond investing, with women more likely to choose certainty when faced with a financial gamble.When it comes to how women invest, Fleming says they are deliberately more cautious."Women are often accused of being more risk adverse, we call it more risk aware," she says. "Certainly from speaking to male investors their main focus is on the rate of return."Fleming also says women appear to invest more broadly. "Men are more likely to invest in technology companies for their higher potential returns, whereas women want to invest in a broader range, from retail to food and drink, health and beauty, fem tech and creative industries."Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at financial services company Hargreaves Lansdown, agrees that women choose the companies they invest in carefully."Women appear to place relatively greater weight on where their money is going and what impact it might have, as well as the reassurance that an investment is right for them," she says."Our research suggests men are...more readily attracted by the potential financial return."Jemma Slingo, pensions and investment specialist at investment firm Fidelity International, says female investors "appear more likely to connect investing with real-life goals, from building emergency savings to looking after children."It's important to remember women in the UK generally have less money to invest than men because the continuing gender pay gap means they earn less on average.Macdonald says that the investment sector "needs to do a better job of making investing feel accessible, relevant and connected to people's own goals and values"."Addressing this would be good for women's long-term financial resilience and for the UK economy."Get in touchAre you affected by issues covered in this story?

schema.headline: 'I started in my 20s and made £8,000': Why women are often better investors than men

title: Bonnie Tyler's celebration of life attended by fans in Mumbles
description: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets as coffin taken to Swansea homeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fans of the singer placed flow
body: Thousands of Bonnie Tyler fans line the streets as coffin taken to Swansea homeImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fans of the singer placed flowers on the hearse carrying her coffin ByOlivia GristBBC WalesReporting fromreporting from MumblesLegendary singer Bonnie Tyler has made a final journey to her Mumbles home, with thousands of emotional fans lining the streets to pay their respects.The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a hospital in Portugal.At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.Despite Tyler's career taking her all over the world, she has been described by those living in the coastal suburb of Mumbles as a "Swansea girl through and through", and someone who "never forgot where she came from".Huge crowds turned out as her coffin was driven through the place she called home.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Thousands of fans gathered as Bonnie Tyler's coffin made its way through Mumbles in SwanseaAs the procession began, Total Eclipse of the Heart could be heard playing on the busy street, as crying fans broke into applause.The coffin was draped in the Welsh flag and accompanied by a framed photograph of the singer, whose real name was Gaynor Sullivan.Fans threw flowers on to the hearse as it drove down Newton Road.Thousands of fans followed the coffin as it made its way through the street, continuing to walk behind it until the end of the road.Figure caption, Bonnie Tyler fans lined the streets as her coffin returned to her Swansea home"She was lovely - just like a friend you'd known all of your life," said Angela Powell who was among the first to arrive."My mam used to cut Gaynor's husband Bobbie's hair and so he would let her into the nightclubs [which he managed] in the town without having to queue. "She actually met my father in one of them, The Townsend, where Bonnie would regularly perform. "My father is unwell so my mam is home looking after him and can't be here, so I wanted to come on behalf of us all to thank her. "I've met her a few times - in Marks and Spencer and on a flight to Portugal."Image caption, Angela Powell described Tyler as "like a friend you've known all your life" Andrea Witts from Bryncoch and Maggie Phillips from Gorseinon said they both grew up with Tyler's music and wanted to honour her."Many years ago I worked in Skewen and taught her niece," said Maggie."The whole family were lovely. I would often bump into her in local shops and restaurants and was she was always lovely."Image caption, The Total Eclipse of the Heart singer died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a hospital in PortugalThe celebration of Tyler's life will continue from midday on Monday, at St Mary's Church in Swansea. She'll then return to her hometown in Neath Port Talbot, travelling through the village at about 13:20 BST before a private family service.A funeral notice from William Pressdee Funeralcare, on behalf of Tyler's family, said she would be remembered as "a warm, generous artist whose music touched generations and continues to fill dance floors and karaoke booths around the world".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The streets were filled with emotional fansSabine Neumann and her son Enrico arrived from Berlin, Germany, on Friday to attend the tribute and Monday's service.Enrico said his mother had also been a Tyler fan so he began listening to her music as a child."It's so special to be here with my mother," he said."She's been very emotional about sharing this opportunity with me.Image caption, Sabine Neumann and her son Enrico have arrived from Berlin to pay tributeThe mother and son had tickets to see Bonnie Tyler perform live in November this year in Berlin."My mother has seen her live all across Germany", Enrico said, "but I never got the chance to which is why this was even more special for me".Monika Macleod-Elliott from Basingstoke said: "I grew up with her music, but never was fortunate to see her live so coming here today was a way of saying goodbye and paying my respects. "I think it's going to be emotional but we're celebrating and she'd want us to be singing along and happy."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption,  Total Eclipse of the Heart singer Bonnie Tyler's funeral will be held on MondayTyler, born Gaynor Hopkins, grew up in a council house in Neath, and is survived by her husband of more than 50 years, Robert Sullivan.She was discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a club in Swansea, and released her first single Lost in France in 1977.Image caption, Foral tributes and messages have been placed outside Tyler's homesIt's a Heartache, her country-pop ballad released the same year, reached number four on the UK singles chart and number three on the US Billboard Hot 100.Her biggest hit, the rockier Total Eclipse of the Heart, arrived six years later in 1983 - this time topping the charts on both sides of the Atlantic.In doing so she became the first Welsh person to score a number one hit in the US.She received a Grammy nomination for the hit, and two further nominations for the album Faster Than the Speed of Night and the single Here She Comes.

schema.headline: Bonnie Tyler's celebration of life attended by fans in Mumbles

title: From making friends to managing money: Students' advice for this year's freshers
description: Image source, Tom Werner/Getty ImagesImage caption, While they were excited to start university, students say they worried about budgeting, making fri
body: Image source, Tom Werner/Getty ImagesImage caption, While they were excited to start university, students say they worried about budgeting, making friends and being homesickByGrace DeanYou've got your A-level results, your university place has been confirmed, and you're applying for student finance.For many, the weeks before starting university are filled with excitement about exploring a new city, meeting new friends and studying a subject you love. But in the back of your mind, you also might be feeling a bit anxious.With a record number of 18-year-olds expected to start university this year, BBC News asked current students about the worries they had before arriving, how they overcame them, and what advice they'd give to freshers feeling uncertain about taking the next step.Nervous about meeting new people?For Isaak Hewitt, moving to Cardiff for university - where he knew no-one - was a "completely blank slate".The idea of meeting lots of new people for the first time since starting secondary school was nerve-racking he says, but Isaak made friends by talking to people he met at lectures and seminars. Now aged 20, Isaak says he was sometimes "terrified" trying to strike up conversations, but the fact everyone was studying English together gave them common ground.He advises freshers to act confident - even if you're scared inside - and to put yourself out there.Image source, EF Volart/Getty ImagesImage caption, Many people say making friends is one of their biggest worries about starting uniAs a commuter student in Nottingham, Grace Morrell was also worried about how she'd meet people, when others were making friends through their halls and student flats. Instead, Grace says she met new people by joining her student magazine, and the radio and theatre societies."A lot of my friendships come from putting myself out there and just doing what I love, which I found was a bit hard at times, especially when you don't know anyone," says Grace, 19.'I worked really hard and it paid off': Elation, nerves and proud parents as students get resultsAre the UK's top universities really 'hoovering up' students?Lots of students try to connect with future coursemates and flatmates on social media before they start university, like Mustafa Dassu, 19, who says freshers' WhatsApp chats helped him make friends before he started at King's College London."Everyone was typing on them all the time between that period of results day and freshers' itself," Mustafa says, "and I met friends that I'm still in touch with a lot today."Anxious about feeling homesick?"I really worried about having to be on my own," says Izzy Garcez, 20, who thought she would miss spending evenings with her family and having people to eat and watch TV with.But in the end she wasn't as homesick as she'd anticipated."Realistically, you'll make friends so quickly at uni," Izzy says, "and you're going to get to a point where you realise 'I've not called my parents in a week', and you'll realise that suddenly you're not actually missing them anymore - or not missing them nearly as much." Concerned about managing your money?Image source, Kieran MillerImage caption, Kieran says it's important to remember your maintenance loan has to last until the next instalmentJournalism student Kieran Miller was worried about money, but he compared student bank accounts and chose one that gave him a free 16-25 Railcard, and signed up for student discount schemes.Everything you need to know about university costsThough it might be exciting to see your first maintenance loan payment hit your bank account in one big lump sum, Kieran, 19, says you need to remember it has to last until the next instalment.With the help of his mum, Kieran, from Swansea, made a provisional budget before moving away, but warns that it's easy to get caught up in the student experience and spend more than you planned to."When you start uni and you're living away from your family and you've got this new sense of freedom it was also really difficult to stay strict financially because you want to make mates with people," he says. "Someone might invite you to go for food or to go for a drink - and you're like, 'I don't really want to say no because this is a chance to connect with someone.'"As well as student loans, most universities offer a variety of scholarships and bursaries, and it's worth checking whether you're eligible.Will you be able to juggle it all?Many students balance classes and studying alongside part-time work, volunteering, sports clubs and societies.Before starting her English and drama degree, Avery Hewitt, 19, worried about juggling studying with working and playing in a university band. She says speaking online to a student ambassador about the workload helped her manage her expectations.Avery also advises new students to be realistic about their timetable and how much they can take on. "I threw myself into everything in the first semester, which I quickly figured out was too much to handle," Avery says, "so I had to make responsible choices about what societies or club nights I needed to cut back on."Not sure you've picked the right course?Image source, Pia SubongImage caption, Pia switched from biochemistry to film and EnglishEven though your place is now confirmed, it's still not too late to change your mind. You can contact your university before you start to ask about changing course, or you can apply for courses at other universities through clearing.After she started at the University of East Anglia, Pia Subong, 21, says she realised that biochemistry wasn't the right course for her and so switched to film and English.If you're having doubts about whether the course is right for you, "you're having these feelings for a reason," Pia says.Image source, Fatima QureshiImage caption, Fatima says taking a gap year was the right decision for herYou can also take a gap year, as Fatima Qureshi, 19, from London did - because she wasn't sure which course she wanted to do or which career path she'd enjoy.Fatima eventually decided to study law, but if she had chosen a course the year previously she'd likely have opted for biochemistry or pharmacy."It was the best thing I could have done," she says.Feeling anxious about starting?It's natural to feel anxious, according to Mel Kennedy, student wellbeing adviser at Ulster University, who says change "can be scary" and lots of people experience "fear of the unknown"."For many students, starting university is the first time that they're stepping into a genuinely unknown environment," agrees Lindsay While, assistant director for student wellbeing and welfare at Teesside University."Many students do experience anxiety and uncertainty because it is such a major transition, but everybody's experience is completely different."Universities offer a range of practical and wellbeing services, including budgeting advice, financial support, counselling and study support sessions. You can also reach out to the university if you need support before you start.What if university isn't for you?Some people told BBC News university had felt like the expected next step after sixth form or college. But Aashi Soni, 20, from Leicester, knew it wasn't right for her."Your college and sixth form don't really push you down that path [of apprenticeships] like they do with university and I found it really difficult," Aashi says. She turned down her university offers and took a gap year to find a suitable apprenticeship.In the end, Aashi started a Level 6 degree apprenticeship in sales at Coca-Cola Europacific Partners. She says it has helped her grow in confidence, gain real-life experience while studying, and get mentoring.Image source, Aashi Soni and Meenu HettigamaImage caption, Aashi and Meenu say university is often presented as the default option - but it wasn't right for themMeenu Hettigama, 21, from Walsall began a creative media course after leaving school, but soon dropped out and applied for apprenticeships instead. She is now two years into a management degree apprenticeship at Amazon."University is not the only pathway," Meenu says, "even if maybe you think it's the most conventional or it is what your family want you to do."You can search for apprenticeships on the UK government, Welsh government, Northern Ireland government and apprenticeships.scot websites. You can also find apprenticeships on sites like LinkedIn and Indeed and at apprenticeship recruitment events.

schema.headline: From making friends to managing money: Students' advice for this year's freshers

title: Men are turning to penis fillers, but are they safe?
description: What's driving men to get penis fillers, despite the risks?Image source, Getty ImagesByInside Health presenter, BBC Radio 4Jason didn't want a "Coke c
body: What's driving men to get penis fillers, despite the risks?Image source, Getty ImagesByInside Health presenter, BBC Radio 4Jason didn't want a "Coke can" – that's the nickname for a penis that has been enlarged with so much filler it resembles a stubby drink can."Some people go really overboard," Jason tells me when we meet in Manchester.His procedure increased the girth of his penis by 16% - an amount he, and his partner, are really happy with. He says it has given him a "self-confidence boost"."Everything still functions" as normal, Jason explains - just with "that extra little bit of width".It is not clear how many men like Jason are having penis fillers. And you can't walk down the street and get a sense of it in the way you can visibly see the popularity of lip fillers. There is little regulation and there are no official records as anybody can start offering the procedure.Penis fillers even became the topic of a bizarre conspiracy theory at the last Winter Olympics. Male ski jumpers were rumoured to be using fillers to increase the surface area of their suits so they could jump further.However, some men have ended up in A&E with a penis turning black and skin "sloughing off" after a botched procedure. And the British Association of Urological Surgeons has issued warnings to men having these procedures.So why are men doing it and what are the risks?Why are men getting penis fillers?Inside HealthInside HealthJames Gallagher visits a private clinic to find out about about the procedure, meets a man who has had it done, and chats to a surgeon who says he is dealing with the consequences when it goes wrong.Jason talked to us frankly, but anonymously, about his decision to have fillers.He was happy with the length of his penis but wanted a "bit more symmetry" and more girth to "get that nice, balanced look"."If you feel like it's a bit lacking," Jason says, "then, why not?"He spent a year weighing up options and ruled out having a surgical procedure. He chose a type of filler - hyaluronic acid - that is temporary so he knew that even if he hated the look it would "eventually just dissolve".Jason says he wasn't motivated by swaggering alpha masculinity - "I don't subscribe to 'how big your dick is, is how big of a man you are'". Rather, he says expectations of male beauty have shifted."It's not just women that need to keep up, men need to keep up as well."It's literally just society changing. I think the way the media portrays everything has a massive impact on everyday life now," he says. "It's like you can't actually go anywhere without seeing some picture-perfect somebody."Trawl the websites of clinics offering penis enlargement - which ask questions like "are you embarrassed by the size of your penis?" - and you can see how some tap into this.There are a variety of penis-enhancement options. There are surgical and non-surgical techniques and different materials that can be injected into the penis.Most common by far is injecting the gel-like substance hyaluronic acid - the same key ingredient used in lip fillers.Hyaluronic acid is a naturally occurring sugar molecule in the body and is known as a "moisture magnet" as it grabs hold of water.Image source, BBC/James GallagherImage caption, Dr Javed Hussain performs a range of cosmetic procedures, including penis fillersDr Javed Hussain has been offering penis fillers for more than a year at his clinic in Prestwich, Greater Manchester.Hussain trained as a doctor before moving into cosmetic procedures, but penis fillers do not legally require any medical training to perform. He says demand is increasing. He's treated men of all ages - some in their mid-20s, while his oldest client is aged 72.The process starts with consultations on the patient's health, reasons for wanting to have the procedure, expectations about the results, and a discussion about the risks.On the day of the event itself, a penis is injected with hyaluronic acid three times - on the top and on either side. The hyaluronic acid filler is delivered through a cannula that enters at the base and travels along the length of the shaft.Image source, BBC/James GallagherImage caption, The equipment needed, including cannulas and syringe, to perform a penis filler procedure The filler is then massaged to give an even look, which the patient continues as home.At a cost of up to £3,500, Hussain says men can expect between 10% and 20% more girth for the next six to nine months.But there are risks. These range from relatively minor ones such as soreness, bruising and uneven filler, to serious ones including infection. These risks apply to all procedures using filler. However, there is also a risk of damaging the vital structures and blood vessels in the penis that are needed for an erection.  When asked why he feels comfortable offering procedures that are concerning surgeons, Hussain says he "totally understands" why some are worried. "It comes from the right place, that nervousness," he says, "but at the same time, more and more evidence is growing and we're getting the results" and that "there is a benefit" to men.Hussain says he has an "immediate action plan" including drugs to quickly dissolve the filler in the event that things go wrong, and reports that "thankfully, we've never needed to" - although the BBC cannot independently corroborate that.But he recalls one patient who came to him for advice after treatment elsewhere, which had "really gone wrong".He says the incorrect type of filler had been used and the "shaft of the penis was starting to become black" as the procedure had damaged the blood vessels in the penis and the skin was dying. The man was sent straight to A&E.Image source, BBC/James GallagherImage caption, Prof Vaibhav Modgil has seen men for whom penis enhancement procedures have gone wrongProf Vaibhav Modgil, an andrologist and consultant urological surgeon for the NHS in Manchester, has seen these men coming into hospital after botched procedures."When it does happen, it can be devastating for the patient," he says.He recalls seeing men with "skin necrosis, where an area of the skin dies off it turns very black and then it sort of sloughs off."So, men will go in thinking, 'Oh, it's gonna be brilliant', but they might come out actually being even more dissatisfied than when they went in."Alex, who did not want his real name to be used, travelled to Germany for a different type of penis enhancement procedure.He had surgery to cut the ligament that attaches the penis to the pubic bone to make it appear longer. He also had his own fat cells harvested and injected into his penis to enlarge it.When he woke up after the procedure, he was in so much pain he couldn't stand."I sustained a lot of bruising and all my upper legs turned yellow," Alex says. "I couldn't walk properly for about a month."Alex was treated in Modgil's clinic where eventually he was given the all-clear. "Many people do not get that luxury," he says. "I got off lucky."Alex says he knows he was "never small in the first place", but society and porn had convinced him that a bigger penis was "masculine and the best".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, There is a lack of data on how fillers affect the penis long-termDespite a lack of official data on the number of penile enhancement procedures, Modgil says online search trends, advertising and social media all "points to the fact that the numbers are on the up". This has led the British Association of Urological Surgeons to issue new recommendations against these procedures."The guidance that we've recently produced essentially says we cannot recommend that any of these procedures should take place because the evidence is so poor," says Modgil.It looked at 36 studies, involving 3,750 men, but said it was still not clear what the "safety profile" of these procedures were.This is partly down to a lack of data on how fillers affect the penis long-term. But there is also concern that - just like lip fillers - you do not need any qualifications to perform the procedure.Modgil says an outright ban is "probably too severe", but if these procedures are going to continue then the industry "massively needs regulation".He called for a national registry to record when penis filler procedures have been performed and for long-term data to be collected so men can make an informed decision based on the risks and the benefits.Back in Manchester, Jason is happy with the results of his procedure and thinks he'll do it again when his current fillers wear off.Inside Health was produced by Gerry Holt.

schema.headline: Men are turning to penis fillers, but are they safe?
